title: How to log in to Wi-Fi requiring web authentication on screenless devices? A Raspberry Pi temporary MAC experiment tutorial
subtitle: Understand the devices and scenarios, prepare the necessary items, and then conduct the experiment in order
description: Starting from common devices such as smart speakers, Wi-Fi cameras, and robot vacuums, this article explains web authentication scenarios in campus dormitories, hotels, and apartments, along with the required items and Raspberry Pi experiment steps.
markdown:
In school dormitories, hotels, or apartments with unified network services, you may have encountered the following situation: after connecting your phone to Wi-Fi, you open a webpage, enter your account number or verification code, and then gain internet access; smart devices also connect to Wi-Fi, but there is no place to open this login webpage. This additional webpage is commonly known as the **Portal authentication page**. This article discusses a compatibility experiment: allowing the Raspberry Pi to temporarily use the wireless network card address (MAC) of the target device, with the author completing the webpage login; after the Raspberry Pi exits, observe whether the target device can directly access the internet. > Only for personal devices and personal accounts, and must be permitted by the network administrator. The script already includes offline checks; actual MAC switching, Portal login, and whether the device can inherit authentication still require real-machine verification. [Project source code ](https://github.com/Xplore-LAB/portal-mac-experiment) · [Download experiment package v0.3.2 ](https://github.com/Xplore-LAB/portal-mac-experiment/releases/download/v0.3.2/portal-mac-experiment-v0.3.2.zip) · [Complete technical tutorial ](https://github.com/Xplore-LAB/portal-mac-experiment/blob/v0.3.2/TUTORIAL.md) ## 1. Which devices and scenarios encounter this? "Screenless smart devices" are present in daily life, for example: - **Smart speakers:** Play online music, check weather, voice Q&A, usually set up Wi-Fi via a mobile app. - **Wi-Fi cameras:** Such as indoor or pet cameras, which use corresponding remote viewing functions after connecting to the network. - **Robot vacuums:** Operate remotely and view cleaning records through the manufacturer's app. - **Smart plugs, light bulbs, and other devices with direct Wi-Fi connectivity:** Configure and use networking features via the mobile app. Their common characteristic is: **they can connect to the network but may not have a browser to complete web-based authentication.** Some products feature small displays but cannot open web pages, and may encounter the same issues. Whether a specific model is applicable still requires individual verification; products that use only Bluetooth or connect via a gateway should be evaluated based on their actual networking method. Common scenarios include **campus dormitories, long-term rental apartments and employee dormitories, hotels, or homestays**: the network may require entering a student ID, phone number, room number, or confirming terms. **Shared workspaces and temporary exhibition booths** authorized by the venue operator may also encounter similar issues, particularly when demonstration devices connect to guest Wi-Fi. The current script targets networks where **the Wi-Fi itself requires no password for connection, followed by web-based authentication**. Networks requiring an initial Wi-Fi password, as well as 802.1X / WPA-Enterprise networks, are outside the scope of support for this version. You should also verify the frequency bands supported by the device, for example, whether the target network provides 2.4 GHz or 5 GHz bands that the device can use. If the school or venue already has an "IoT device registration" system, an "IoT dedicated network," or if the device's app includes built-in functionality for connecting to hotel or campus networks, use the official entry point first. You can refer to [example of university device registration ](https://it.cornell.edu/wifi/register-device-doesnt-have-browser) and [example of official device access ](https://support.apple.com/guide/homepod/set-up-homepod-apd779d9bb45/homepod)]. ## II. Prepare Items and Operation Channels The items needed are not complicated: - **The target smart device and its power supply**, and locate its actual Wi-Fi MAC address. - **A Raspberry Pi that can boot normally**, including Wi-Fi capability, power supply, and storage media with the operating system installed. The system must use NetworkManager, which is the network management tool corresponding to the `nmcli` command mentioned later. - **A smartphone and the device's companion app (as needed)**, used to select the Wi-Fi for the device and view device information. - **A stable method for operating the Raspberry Pi**, along with the target Wi-Fi name (SSID) and your personal web login credentials. **Operating next to the Raspberry Pi:** Connect a monitor and keyboard; use a mouse when using the graphical desktop. Run the script directly in the terminal on the Raspberry Pi itself. **Operating from a computer:** Connect the computer and Raspberry Pi with a dedicated Ethernet cable, and control it via SSH. This article uses Windows as an example. **The management connection must remain available while the Raspberry Pi switches Wi-Fi**; if SSH is maintained only through the Wi-Fi network interface being modified, the script will refuse to continue. For a direct Ethernet connection on Windows, use `192.168.88.1/24` (computer) and `192.168.88.2/24` (Raspberry Pi). Do not set a default gateway for the management Ethernet cable; first ensure this subnet does not conflict with existing networks. Using another existing control path on the Raspberry Pi, complete the configuration according to the [connection guide ](https://github.com/Xplore-LAB/portal-mac-experiment/blob/v0.3.2/docs/connection-methods.md)], and confirm that you can execute the following commands before starting the experiment: ```powershell ssh myuser@192.168.88.2 ``` Replace `myuser` with the username you set when installing the system. For a newly installed system, you can use the default user and SSH preset by Raspberry Pi Imager; writing the image will erase the SD card, so for an existing system, please confirm and back up first. If you want to operate the Raspberry Pi desktop on Windows, you can configure VNC in a system with a desktop environment and connect via the wired management address; specific steps are also in the connection guide. ## 3. Perform an experiment in sequence The most important aspect of the entire process is the sequence: the target device goes offline first, the Raspberry Pi completes the test, then the Raspberry Pi exits, and finally the target device is started. **First check the target device's MAC address, then ensure it is completely offline.** You can check the device's companion app, the device list on a private router, or have the device connect to a personal hotspot and view connected devices. A MAC address looks like `aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff`, which is different from an IP address like `192.168.1.20`. Some devices use different random MAC addresses on different Wi-Fi networks; try to confirm the actual address it uses on the target network. **Download and transfer to the Raspberry Pi.** When using a monitor, you can copy and extract via a USB drive; when using SSH, run the following in the directory containing the ZIP file in Windows PowerShell: ```powershell scp .\portal-mac-experiment-v0.3.2.zip myuser@192.168.88.2: ssh myuser@192.168.88.2 ``` **The following changes to run in the Raspberry Pi terminal: check first, then start:** ```bash unzip portal-mac-experiment-v0.3.2.zip cd portal-mac-experiment bash quick-start.sh --check bash quick-start.sh ``` Start the script using a regular user, which will call `sudo nmcli` as needed; do not wrap the entire boot process in `sudo` to avoid losing SSH connection information. The default wireless interface is `wlan0`; other names can be used with `WIFI_IF=wlan1 bash quick-start.sh`. **Fill in the prompts and log in yourself.** Enter the target MAC address when first setting up the Wi-Fi name, and complete the necessary confirmations. The script then creates a temporary connection, verifies the actual MAC, IPv4 address, and network exit. If a graphical desktop is present, it will attempt to open a webpage; after confirming it is the network's official authentication page, personally enter your account, password, or verification code. When there is no graphical desktop, you must first prepare an authentication method approved by the network administrator, such as using VNC via a separate management network; for a pure SSH environment, see the [connection guide ](https://github.com/Xplore-LAB/portal-mac-experiment/blob/v0.3.2/docs/connection-methods.md) for optional browser channels. If authentication cannot be completed, stop here and do not treat "connecting to Wi-Fi" as "having internet access". **After completing or giving up, return to the terminal to clean up.** Press Enter as guided to stop the connectivity test and delete temporary configurations. If an error occurs midway, you can manually run: ```bash bash scripts/portal-mac.sh restore ``` `restore` will clean up the connectivity test, **but does not guarantee that the network card's MAC address will immediately revert to its original state, nor will it automatically reconnect to the previous Wi-Fi**. Only after confirming that the Raspberry Pi has exited, allow the target device to reconnect to the same Wi-Fi; if uncertain, shut down the Raspberry Pi first. Temporary Wi-Fi configurations reside only in memory and will disappear after NetworkManager restarts. ## 4. How to determine the result and handle issues? Record the following items separately to know at which step the experiment stopped: | Observed Result | What It Indicates | |---|---| | The actual wireless MAC address matches the target address | MAC switching is effective, but this does not yet indicate that authentication has been passed. | | The test Wi-Fi is connected and has obtained an IPv4 address | Network association is successful; you can proceed to verify the exit and authentication. | | The Raspberry Pi completes the web login, and test traffic indeed accesses the internet via the test Wi-Fi | The Raspberry Pi's authentication was successful this time. | | After the Raspberry Pi exits, the target device can access the internet without web-based operations | The device authentication inheritance was successful this time. | | The target device can still access the internet after reboot | The test after reboot is valid; the authentication duration is still determined by the network. | The script only checks for `1.1.1.1`'s IPv4 routing. Authentication servers, browser proxies, VPNs, and IPv6 may have different paths, so you must also confirm that the actual authentication requests and test traffic traverse the target Wi-Fi. **Wi-Fi switch caused SSH disconnect:** The management connection may still rely on the wireless interface that is pending modification. Establish a local terminal or independent wired connection first, then continue troubleshooting. **The Raspberry Pi can access the internet, but the target device still cannot:** The network may still be bound to an IP address, access location, or session. Record the results, then consult the device access method provided by the network administrator; a single successful connection does not mean authentication is permanently valid. **The device can access the internet, but the mobile app cannot find it:** Guest networks may prevent devices from seeing each other. Device discovery, screen mirroring, and multi-device linkage require separate testing; refer to [Google's official troubleshooting guide](https://support.google.com/chromecast/answer/7566322?hl=en). Use [the results template](https://github.com/Xplore-LAB/portal-mac-experiment/blob/v0.3.2/experiments/result-template.yaml) to save sanitized observations. Do not publicly disclose real MAC addresses, personal addresses, account passwords, Cookies, or Tokens. The quick entry only persistently saves the SSID; runtime configurations and terminal outputs may still contain MAC addresses and IPs; browsers may also save login information separately. For more details on system preparation, VNC, step-by-step commands, and manual recovery, see [the full tutorial](https://github.com/Xplore-LAB/portal-mac-experiment/blob/v0.3.2/TUTORIAL.md). Official references: [Raspberry Pi Initialization](https://www.raspberrypi.com/documentation/computers/getting-started.html), [SSH / VNC](https://www.raspberrypi.com/documentation/computers/remote-access.html), [NetworkManager Commands](https://networkmanager.dev/docs/api/latest/nmcli.html).
